query:
Context: an aluminum melt made by adding AA4047 (Al-12Si) to AA6063 (Al-0.4Si-0.7Mg) was atomized into spherical powder, and we want to test how well the melt mixed by measuring Si with SEM-EDS (Thermo Fisher Apreo FE-SEM, EDAX Octane Plus silicon drift detector, 35 degree take-off angle, standards-based quantification in NIST DTSA-II against pure Al, Si and MgO standards) on powder sampled from the top, middle and bottom of the collection jar. What does it take to resolve a 1 wt% difference in Si (for example 5 versus 6 wt% Si) between two powder lots at 95% confidence?

Cover quantitatively, with citations and DOIs:
(1) Counting statistics: Ziebold's analytical-sensitivity / minimum-detectable-concentration-difference criterion (Anal. Chem. 1967) and its form in Goldstein et al. (Scanning Electron Microscopy and X-ray Microanalysis); modern SDD-EDS precision and repeatability for major and minor elements (e.g. Newbury & Ritchie); how many Si K-alpha counts per spectrum are needed, and whether counting statistics or other error sources dominate at this level.
(2) Unpolished loose spherical particles versus epoxy-mounted, polished cross-sections: magnitude of particle geometric effects (mass, absorption, fluorescence) on Si K-alpha k-ratios and concentrations, given that Si K-alpha (1.74 keV) is strongly absorbed by Al (just above the Al K edge); how much normalization to 100% or peak-to-background ratio methods (Statham; Small et al.) reduce the errors; accuracy and precision reported for particle analysis versus flat polished specimens; recommended particle size relative to the electron interaction volume at 5, 10 and 15-20 kV.
(3) Within-particle microstructural heterogeneity of rapidly solidified hypoeutectic Al-Si powder (alpha-Al cells or dendrites with eutectic Si, supersaturated solid solution) and the raster/area size or number of spots needed for a representative per-particle mean composition.
(4) Sampling statistics: how many particles per lot must be analyzed given particle-to-particle compositional variation; whether composition correlates with particle size in atomized aluminum alloy powders; segregation of powder by particle size in containers and during sampling (riffling, sample splitting), and how that could create an apparent top-versus-bottom composition difference.
(5) Published examples of EDS or electron-probe microanalysis used to assess chemical homogeneity of atomized or blended alloy powders, and how such results compared with bulk methods (ICP-OES, XRF, or X-ray diffraction lattice-parameter/phase-fraction measurements).
Note honestly where the literature is silent or values conflict.
